newsitem.title: FRANCE: Suspense heightens before Ferre's last Dior show.
newsitem.headline: Suspense heightens before Ferre's last Dior show.

text.p: - Italian designer Gianfranco Ferre bid farewell to Paris on Tuesday, but the fashion community was too busy guessing who will succeed him at the house of Christian Dior to care.
Ferre, hired at Dior in 1987, was due to unveil his final collection for the famous label later in the day before returning to Milan to devote himself to his own prospering fashion house.
To heighten the suspense, Dior officials said the choice of a new designer will not be announced until next week.
Speculation has been rife in recent weeks, and French and British medias have tipped John Galliano, Britain's devilish romantic named at Givenchy last year, as Ferre's successor.
If the reports are verified, the job will be open at Givenchy whose prim and proper styles have turned under Galliano into some of the most wild, sexy and theatrical clothes around.
The fashion press thinks another Briton, the subversive Alexander McQueen, will have the job of keeping the prestigious, 40-year-old label on fashion's sharpest edge.
The big question fashion watchers are asking is: would McQueen, who fancies blood stains -- real -- human hair and insects to decorate his creations, be up to the job?

Meanhwhile, Tuesday's shows featured Japan's Junko Shimada sending out plaid Madras cotton over-sized trousers and pareos swaddling the hips like baby blankets, in an odd marriage with fuzzy angora peasant blouses or ruffled transparent polka dot blouses.
There was more sheer chiffon, printed with the African heads for skimpy gowns and open blouses over bare breasts, or pretty white eyelet lace nighties, bloomers and midriffs.
Pinstripe suits, which every self-respecting Paris designer has shown within the last year, here were classic and loosely tailored with long Carnaby street-style coats or jackets.
As for Swiss designer Bertrand Marechal, he never gives up.
The absence of money and interested buyers never keeps him from putting out a collection of slinky, sophisticated evening wear season after season, albeit by the skin of his teeth.
Marechal sews his clothes at home and, this year, presented the collection there -- in his apartment which also serves as an atelier and showroom in Paris' wholesale clothing district.
Featuring just 15 outfits inspired by 1970s New York party girls, the show was a sign that times are harder than ever.

Long crepe togas were slit all the way up the side but for a safety pin at the waist, a skirt and blouse of black faille were encrusted with lace, and a chocolate sheath had a gaping hole in the center that revealed the navel and breast bottoms, stopping just short of the nipples.
One model strolled out in a loud orange satin tank top and scarlet bellbottoms, then languidly drank from a soft drink can.
Rarely has a fashion designer struggled so stubbornly. With a small but devoted group of faithfuls, Marechal has managed to stay in the fashion world's conciousness year in and out.

"It was a catastrophe show -- things are so difficult now, we did it with almost nothing," he apologised. "The inspiration is very much Studio 54, socialites who are neurotic but always very happy and ready to have fun."
